source_file: How Perceived Lack of Benevolence Harms Trust of Artificial Intelligence Management.pdf

entities.name: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Management
entities.description: Computational systems that serve a management role, making executive decisions that influence workers.

entities.name: Employees / Subordinates
entities.description: Individuals who are managed by human or AI systems within an organization.

entities.name: Human Management
entities.description: Traditional human supervisors and managers overseeing employees.

concepts.name: Perceived Benevolence
concepts.description: The belief that a trustee has a positive orientation toward the trustor and a genuine desire to do good for them, beyond egocentric motives.

concepts.name: Trust
concepts.description: The willingness of a subordinate to be vulnerable to a manager based on positive expectations of the manager's actions and intentions.

concepts.name: Empathy Demand
concepts.description: The extent to which an individual expects or wants a counterpart (such as a manager) to vicariously experience and understand the emotions they are feeling.

concepts.name: Emotions as Social Information (EASI) model
concepts.description: A theoretical framework suggesting that emotional expressions provide information to observers about the expresser's feelings, motives, and intentions.

claims: AI management is perceived as less benevolent than human management because AI lacks the authentic capacity to experience emotions.
Employees have lower trust in AI managers compared to human managers.
Perceptions of benevolence mediate the negative relationship between AI (versus human) management and employee trust.
The negative impact of AI management on perceived benevolence and trust is exacerbated in high empathy demand contexts compared to low empathy demand contexts.
summary: This article explores the impact of replacing human managers with AI on employee trust. Through a field study of delivery riders in China and three experiments, the authors demonstrate that AI managers are perceived as less benevolent than human managers because they lack the ability to genuinely experience emotions. This perceived lack of benevolence significantly reduces employees' trust in AI management. Furthermore, the research shows that this negative effect is stronger in work contexts that demand high empathy. The findings highlight the critical role of emotional capability and benevolence in human-to-AI interactions in the workplace.
